Reproducing Pasquereau & Turner (2013) from dandiset 001636¶

Paper. Pasquereau B, Turner RS (2013). Primary motor cortex of the parkinsonian monkey: altered neuronal responses to muscle stretch. Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience 7:98. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2013.00098. This attempt used the full text (open access, PubMed Central PMC3840326) and its supplementary data sheet, whose table gives the neuronal results of each monkey separately.

Dandiset. DANDI:001636, version 0.260518.1819. The paper (2013) cites no DANDI version. This is the only published version, and the draft differs from it only by its modification date, so it is the version pinned here. The dandiset holds single-unit M1 recordings from two monkeys before and after MPTP, from which three papers were written; this one uses the torque perturbation (muscle stretch) trials.

What can be tested. The files of monkey V (Venus, elbow) mark the torque perturbations, with the joint angle, the torque command and triceps EMG. The files of monkey L (Leu, wrist) mark none, so every claim is tested on monkey V alone, against the paper's monkey V values where it gives them (supplementary table) and against its pooled values otherwise.

Claim Tested
cell-counts: 112 and 159 monkey V cells, 49 and 54 PTNs, 31 and 48 CSNs, 3 dual yes
monkey-l-perturbations: monkey L torque responses blocked (data missing)
baseline-rate: lower resting rate after MPTP in PTNs, not CSNs yes
ptn-faster-than-csn: PTNs fire faster than CSNs before MPTP yes
antidromic-latency: CSN antidromic latency longer after MPTP, PTN unchanged yes
false-positive-rate: the detection threshold's false-positive rate near 0.01 yes
torque-related-fractions: monkey V fractions of torque-related cells yes
prevalence-unchanged: MPTP does not change the fraction of torque-related cells yes
ptn-more-responsive: PTNs respond more often than CSNs yes
one-direction-half: 44% of torque-related cells respond to one direction only yes
excitatory-majority: most responses are increases; PTN balance unchanged yes
magnitude-unchanged: response magnitudes unchanged by MPTP yes
venus-response-magnitudes: monkey V response magnitudes yes
latency-shorter: response latencies shorter after MPTP yes
latency-not-training: latencies do not follow days of training yes
fwhm-shorter-ptn: PTN increases briefer after MPTP yes
dsi-reduced: fewer directional responses after MPTP yes
venus-dsi: monkey V mean DSI yes
dsi-not-baseline: resting rate does not differ between directional categories yes
kinematics-slower: torque-induced movements slower and smaller after MPTP yes
kinematic-latency-unchanged: movement latency unchanged yes
emg-m2-larger: larger long-latency (m2) triceps response after MPTP yes
emg-duration-longer: longer EMG responses after MPTP yes
emg-onset-unchanged: EMG onset unchanged yes
emg-m1-weak: m1 much smaller than m2 yes
velocity-matched-magnitude: magnitudes unchanged in velocity-matched sessions yes
session-correlations: no session-level correlation of PTN latency with velocity or m2 yes
trial-correlations: no trial-level correlation blocked (methods underspecified)

Code read. The paper links no analysis code. The dandiset links its conversion code, catalystneuro/turner-lab-to-nwb, read at commit e80a192917490b50db6871180b6d1d9a24772e35: the NeuroConv interfaces that built the files, notes on the source MATLAB files and tutorial notebooks. It settles how the trialized source data were laid end to end (trials and spikes by the behavioural trial end, analog streams by their sample count), which explains the analog clock drift found in the data check. It holds no analysis of the torque responses, so every method choice here comes from the paper's Methods or is fixed in the claims file.

The claims, with their criteria, are in claims/001636/10.3389-fnsys.2013.00098.yaml. The loading and the measures are in stretch.py, whose docstring says which parameters come from the paper and which were chosen here.

The dandiset holds 447 files with 568 units: 210 of monkey L (Leu) and 358 of monkey V (Venus). The MPTP state in the session id agrees with each unit's is_post_mptp. The dandiset's description says Leu was recorded in 1993; some Leu files are dated 1992.

No monkey L file marks a torque perturbation: torque_perturbation_type is "none" in every Leu trial. The monkey V units with at least 5 perturbations of each direction number 112 before and 159 after MPTP, with 49 and 54 PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs, the monkey V counts of the paper's supplementary table. These units are the cells studied here. The other projection types (thalamic and subthalamic projections) are counted as non-identified (NA) cells, as the paper has no such category, and the dual PTN and CSN units are kept apart from both.

In monkey V the joint moves by more than 2 deg in the hold window in 66% (pre) and 86% (post) of perturbed trials and in 1% and 11% of the others. In monkey L it does so in 15% of trials before MPTP and 1% after, which does not fit perturbations on two thirds of the trials as the Methods describe; these windows were set from the monkey V onsets, so the monkey L perturbations could fall outside them. Either way, the monkey L torque trials cannot be identified from the files, and monkey-l-perturbations is blocked. The Leu torque command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file, and 15 post-MPTP Leu files have no analog data at all. The Leu analog streams are sampled at 100 Hz; the paper says 200 Hz for monkey L. Monkey V is sampled at 1 kHz (the paper digitized at 500 Hz; the conversion notes say the lab interpolated to 1 kHz).

The torque command shows the same. In monkey V a command excursion starts in the hold window in 1811 pre-MPTP and 3563 post-MPTP trials, against 1862 and 3649 labelled perturbations; before MPTP every one of them lasts 40 to 70 ms. In monkey L the command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file, and 35 post-MPTP files hold one. Of their 2048 trials, one has an excursion starting in the hold window (70 ms, 41 units). Their 91 to 413 excursions per file start a median 0.31 to 0.84 s after the lateral target appears, during the active movement. No monkey L file holds a hold-period torque impulse.

venus = [s for s in S if s["subject"] == "Venus" and "windows" in s]
AX = np.arange(stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[0], stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[1] + 1)


def command_onset(w):
    # first ms where the torque command leaves its pre-onset level by more than 6 SD (and 10 units)
    base = np.nanmedian(w[:, :400], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sd = np.nanstd(w[:, :400], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    dev = np.abs(w - base) > np.maximum(10, 6 * sd)
    return np.where(dev.any(1), AX[np.argmax(dev, axis=1)], np.nan)


realigned = np.concatenate([command_onset(s["windows"]["torque_cmd"]) for s in venus])
stored = np.concatenate([command_onset(s["windows"]["torque_cmd_stored"]) for s in venus])
lag = np.concatenate([s["analog_lag_ms"][s["pert_trial"]] for s in venus])
ok = np.isfinite(stored) & np.isfinite(realigned)
print(f"Monkey V perturbations: {len(realigned)}; command step found in {int(np.isfinite(realigned).sum())}")
print("Torque command step relative to the labelled onset, realigned clock (ms), percentiles 1/50/99:",
      np.nanpercentile(realigned, [1, 50, 99]))
print("Same on the stored analog clock (ms), percentiles 1/50/99:", np.nanpercentile(stored, [1, 50, 99]))

The analog streams (angle, torque command, EMG) are not on the clock of the trials table as stored. The conversion lays each trial's analog samples end to end with 3 s gaps, using their sample count, while the trials table and spike times use the behavioural software's trial end, which is a few ms later. The stored analog clock therefore falls behind by about 5 ms per trial, reaching hundreds of ms late in a session, and the torque command step appears up to about 100 ms before the labelled onset (the step time follows the accumulated lag, r = -1.0). With each analog segment moved back to its trial's start (stretch.realign), the command steps 4 to 7 ms after every labelled onset. All analog measures here use the realigned clock. This is a format error of the files: the notes say the analog data end 5 ms early but not that later trials are shifted.

The angle's reference_frame says positive is extension. The values say the reverse: active flexion movements raise the angle by about 18 deg and extension movements lower it, in both monkeys, and flexion torques raise it. The torque labels themselves agree with the EMG (the triceps, an extensor stretched by a flexion torque, responds to flexion torques; see the EMG sections). So the reference frame's sign is wrong, and the series are named "Elbow" also for monkey L, whose task used the wrist.

# Angle scale: active movements measured here (same filter as the torque-evoked movements, around
# derived_movement_onset_time) against the files' derived columns and target amplitudes.
act = pd.concat([s["trials"].assign(subject=s["subject"]) for s in S if "active_peak_velocity" in s["trials"]])
act = act[act.active_peak_velocity.notna() & act.derived_peak_velocity.notna()]
act["ratio_velocity"] = act.active_peak_velocity / act.derived_peak_velocity
act["ratio_amplitude"] = act.active_amplitude / act.derived_amplitude.abs()
print(act.groupby("subject").agg(movements=("ratio_velocity", "size"),
      target_amplitude_median=("target_amplitude", "median"),
      derived_amplitude_median=("derived_amplitude", lambda x: x.abs().median()),
      amplitude_here_median=("active_amplitude", "median"),
      derived_peak_velocity_median=("derived_peak_velocity", "median"),
      peak_velocity_here_median=("active_peak_velocity", "median"),
      ratio_velocity_median=("ratio_velocity", "median"),
      ratio_amplitude_median=("ratio_amplitude", "median")).round(2).to_string())
for subj, g in act.groupby("subject"):
    print(f"{subj}: Spearman rho of peak velocity here against derived_peak_velocity "
          f"{stats.spearmanr(g.active_peak_velocity, g.derived_peak_velocity)[0]:.3f}; "
          f"velocity ratio within 10% of 1 in {((g.ratio_velocity - 1).abs() <= 0.1).mean():.1%}")

The angle's scale agrees with the files' own kinematic columns. Active movements measured here, with the filter used for the torque-evoked movements, have median peak velocities and amplitudes within 2% of derived_peak_velocity and derived_movement_amplitude (median ratios 0.99 to 1.02; Spearman rho 0.989 and 0.993 for peak velocity), and their median amplitude (20.4 deg in monkey V) matches the 20 deg targets. The angle is consistent with degrees, as stated, and the filter keeps the peak velocity of these movements.

# Spikes against the trials table: does the torque direction become decodable from single-cell
# spike counts only after the labelled onset? 20 ms windows, Mann-Whitney flexion vs extension.
edges = np.arange(-200, 201, 20)
studied_v = units[units.studied & (units.subject == "Venus")]
sig = np.zeros(len(edges) - 1)
for r in studied_v.itertuples():
    s, u = S[r.si], S[r.si]["units"][r.ui]
    counts = np.array([np.histogram(x, edges)[0] for x in u["pert"]])
    f, e = counts[s["pert_direction"] == "flexion"], counts[s["pert_direction"] == "extension"]
    for j in range(len(edges) - 1):
        if np.ptp(np.r_[f[:, j], e[:, j]]) > 0:
            sig[j] += stats.mannwhitneyu(f[:, j], e[:, j]).pvalue < 0.01
frac = sig / len(studied_v)
print(f"Fraction of the {len(studied_v)} monkey V cells studied whose spike counts differ between "
      "flexion and extension trials (Mann-Whitney p < 0.01), by window (ms from labelled onset):")
print(pd.Series(frac.round(3), index=[f"{a} to {b}" for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])]).to_string())

The spike times therefore share the trials table's clock to within the 20 ms windows, consistent with the 20 to 60 ms response latencies of the paper.

# Files that repeat another file's recording: same subject and date, and the trial durations of one
# are a contiguous block of the other's.
dur = {si: np.round((s["trials"].stop - s["trials"].start).values, 3) for si, s in enumerate(S)}
repeats = []
for (subj, date), g in sessions.groupby(["subject", "date"]):
    for a in g.si:
        for b in g.si:
            if a != b and len(dur[b]) <= len(dur[a]) and (len(dur[b]) < len(dur[a]) or a < b):
                n = len(dur[b])
                if any(np.array_equal(dur[a][i:i + n], dur[b]) for i in range(len(dur[a]) - n + 1)):
                    repeats.append({"file": sessions.code[a], "repeated_in": sessions.code[b],
                                    "trials": len(dur[a]), "repeated_trials": n,
                                    "units_file": [u["unit_name"] for u in S[a]["units"]],
                                    "units_repeat": [u["unit_name"] for u in S[b]["units"]],
                                    "types_file": [stretch.short_type(u["type"]) for u in S[a]["units"]],
                                    "types_repeat": [stretch.short_type(u["type"]) for u in S[b]["units"]]})
repeats = pd.DataFrame(repeats)
print("Files whose trials repeat a block of another file's trials:")
print(repeats.to_string(index=False))


def trial_spikes(s, u):
    # spike times relative to the start of their trial, one array per trial
    tr = s["trials"]
    k = np.searchsorted(tr.start.values, u["spikes"], side="right") - 1
    return [np.round(u["spikes"][k == i] - tr.start.values[i], 4) for i in range(len(tr))]


same_unit = []
for r in repeats.itertuples():
    a = S[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.file].si.iloc[0])]
    b = S[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.repeated_in].si.iloc[0])]
    da, db = dur[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.file].si.iloc[0])], dur[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.repeated_in].si.iloc[0])]
    off = [i for i in range(len(da) - len(db) + 1) if np.array_equal(da[i:i + len(db)], db)][0]
    for ub in b["units"]:
        tb = trial_spikes(b, ub)
        for ua in a["units"]:
            ta = trial_spikes(a, ua)[off:off + len(db)]
            n_same = sum(np.array_equal(x, y) for x, y in zip(ta, tb))
            same_unit.append({"file": r.file, "unit": ua["unit_name"], "type": ua["type"],
                              "repeat": r.repeated_in, "repeat_unit": ub["unit_name"], "repeat_type": ub["type"],
                              "identical_trials": f"{n_same}/{len(db)}",
                              "spikes_in_block": (sum(map(len, ta)), sum(map(len, tb)))})
same_unit = pd.DataFrame(same_unit)
print("\nUnits of each repeated recording compared trial by trial over the repeated block:")
print(same_unit.to_string(index=False))
dup_units = same_unit[same_unit.identical_trials.str.split("/", regex=False).str[0].astype(int) > 0]

Four monkey V files repeat a block of trials of another file of the same day: the same recording (trials, angle, torque, EMG) is deposited twice. In two of them the repeated file's unit is also in the first file, with identical spikes in every repeated trial, but with another projection type: v4527 unit 2 is "not_tested" and its copy in v4527b is a PTN; v5811 unit 2 is a PTN and its copy in v5812 is "no_response". Which type is right cannot be told from the files. The main analysis keeps every unit as stored, which gives the paper's monkey V counts (so the paper's database may count these two cells twice); a variant drops the two copies in the repeated files. The repeated files are left out of the session measures (kinematics, EMG), so that each recording counts once.

The unit_also_in_session_id column says the unit was recorded in another session, "identified by the experimenter based on waveform similarity". Its references use the prefixes "V" and "L", where the session ids use "Venus" and "Leu", and most referenced files are not in the dandiset. Where the referenced file is present, it holds a unit with another unit number, another spike count and, in several cases, another projection type than the referring unit. These are not the same neuron as stored; the column more likely names the file holding the second unit of the recording. The units are treated as distinct cells, which also gives the paper's counts.

Every unit's spike times are sorted and fall within the trials. The paper verified isolation by a refractory period over 2 ms; a few units have more than 1% of their ISIs below 2 ms, and they are kept, as the dandiset holds the units the paper selected.

EMG units are A/D values stored as arbitrary units, so EMG is compared only within the dandiset. The files describe the EMG as rectified and sample-hold integrated over 10 ms; the paper says rectified and low-pass filtered at 100 Hz.

The torque command differs between the two states. Its 50 ms pulse has three sizes, about 46, 91 and 183 units above the resting level. Most pre-MPTP sessions have the smallest and most post-MPTP sessions the largest (four times the size), with the middle size in some sessions of each state; post-MPTP pulses are also followed by an opposite swing of about a quarter of the pulse. The paper says every impulse was 0.1 Nm for 50 ms. The command is stored in arbitrary units and the files do not give its scale, so whether the torque or only the command's scaling changed cannot be told from the files. Either way the pre and post perturbations are not shown to be the same; the kinematic and EMG claims add a variant restricted to sessions of the middle size, which both states have.

The torque onset follows the appearance of the center target by 1.70 to 1.73 s in 90% of monkey V perturbations. The Methods put it 1 to 2 s, uniformly at random, after the monkey captured the center target. If the column marks the target's appearance, the torque was not unpredictable from it; the column may instead mark a later event. This does not enter any analysis here.

Responses of the cells studied¶

Every monkey V cell studied is analysed once, below, and the claims draw on these tables. For each cell: the single-trial SDFs (causal gamma kernel, k = 1.5, theta = 20 ms), its baseline rate (mean SDF over the 500 ms before onset, all perturbations), and for each direction the response found by the main detection (threshold on the trial-averaged SDF) and by the variant (t-test across trials), at the true onset and at a pseudo onset 600 ms earlier.

In [10]:
cells = units[units.studied & (units.subject == "Venus")].copy().reset_index(drop=True)
resp_rows, base, mean_sdf = [], [], {}
for c in cells.itertuples():
    s, u = S[c.si], S[c.si]["units"][c.ui]
    X = stretch.sdfs(u["pert"])
    base.append(X[:, stretch._mask(*stretch.BASELINE_MS)].mean())
    for d in ("flexion", "extension"):
        Xd = X[s["pert_direction"] == d]
        mean_sdf[(c.Index, d)] = Xd.mean(0)
        for method, shift in (("mean", 0), ("trials", 0), ("mean", stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS),
                              ("trials", stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS)):
            r = stretch.detect(Xd, shift_ms=shift, method=method)
            r.update(cell=c.Index, direction=d, method=method, pseudo=shift != 0)
            resp_rows.append(r)
cells["baseline_rate"] = base
R = pd.DataFrame(resp_rows).merge(cells[["state", "ptype", "si", "date", "duplicate_copy"]],
                                  left_on="cell", right_index=True)
main = R[(R.method == "mean") & ~R.pseudo]
by_cell = main.pivot(index="cell", columns="direction")
cells["torque_related"] = by_cell["responds"].any(axis=1).values
cells["n_directions"] = by_cell["responds"].sum(axis=1).values
cells["latency"] = by_cell["latency"].min(axis=1).values
dsis = [stretch.dsi(main[(main.cell == i) & (main.direction == "flexion")].iloc[0].to_dict(),
                    main[(main.cell == i) & (main.direction == "extension")].iloc[0].to_dict())
        for i in cells.index]
cells["dsi"] = [d for d, _ in dsis]
cells["category"] = [c for _, c in dsis]
resp = main[main.responds].copy()
print(f"{len(cells)} cells studied, {len(main)} cell-directions; responses found: {len(resp)} "
      f"in {int(cells.torque_related.sum())} cells")
flat = main[main.baseline_sd == 0]
print("Cell-directions without a usable baseline (SD of the baseline SDF 0; they can never respond):",
      len(flat), "| by type and state:", flat.groupby(["ptype", "state"]).size().to_dict())
print("Trials per cell and direction: ", main.n_trials.min(), "to", main.n_trials.max(),
      "| baseline rate range", round(cells.baseline_rate.min(), 2), "to", round(cells.baseline_rate.max(), 2), "spikes/s")
print("Response latencies (ms):", resp.latency.min(), "to", resp.latency.max(),
      "| offsets:", resp.offset.min(), "to", resp.offset.max())

cell-counts¶

In monkey V, 112 neurons were studied before MPTP and 159 after, of which 49 and 54 were PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs; three neurons in all were activated from both the peduncle and the putamen.

Dropping the two unit copies changes the post-MPTP PTN count to 53.

monkey-l-perturbations¶

In monkey L, 57 of 115 neurons before MPTP and 35 of 73 after responded to torque perturbations of the wrist.

Blocked: the monkey L files mark no torque perturbation (data check above), so neither the trials nor their onsets can be found. The files hold 138 and 72 monkey L units, against the paper's 115 and 73 cells studied.

baseline-rate¶

Before torque onset, the firing rate of M1 neurons was lower after MPTP, because PTN rates fell (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) while CSN rates did not change (p = 0.5). In monkey V, 12.6 and 8.9 spikes/s for all cells, 20.3 and 14.8 for PTNs, 3.5 and 3.4 for CSNs.

def mwu(a, b):
    return stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided").pvalue

The PTN rate is lower after MPTP (Mann-Whitney p = 0.034) and the CSN rate does not differ (p = 0.73); the M1 rate is lower (p = 0.0033). The statement's p < 0.001 for PTNs, from both monkeys, is not reached in monkey V alone. Dropping the unit copies leaves the PTN result the same (p = 0.034).

ptn-faster-than-csn¶

Before MPTP, PTNs fired much faster than CSNs at rest (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).

antidromic-latency¶

PTN antidromic latencies did not change after MPTP (1.9 ms, p = 0.9), while CSN latencies were longer (5.1 against 6.1 ms, p < 0.05/3).

In [14]:
def antidromic(df, label):
    rows = []
    for g, e in (("PTN", (1.9, 1.9, 0.22, 0.2)), ("CSN", (5.1, 6.1, 0.61, 0.89))):
        sub = df[df.ptype == g]
        a, b = sub[sub.state == "pre"].antidromic_latency_ms.dropna(), sub[sub.state == "post"].antidromic_latency_ms.dropna()
        rows.append({"cells": label, "group": g, "n_pre": len(a), "pre": a.mean(), "sd_pre": a.std(),
                     "in_tol_pre": abs(a.mean() - e[0]) <= e[2], "n_post": len(b), "post": b.mean(),
                     "sd_post": b.std(), "in_tol_post": abs(b.mean() - e[1]) <= e[3], "mwu_p": mwu(a, b)})
    return rows

false-positive-rate¶

The detection threshold, p < 0.01 divided by 5 independent comparisons, holds the chance of a false response over the 200 ms epoch near 0.01.

# from center target to torque onset), so the epoch matches the true one but has no torque.

# Where the false crossings come from. (1) The pseudo-onset rate by baseline rate and by number of
# trials. (2) Stationary Poisson spike trains at each cell-direction's baseline rate, with its number
# of trials, through the same detection: no response exists, so every crossing is false.

# How the result changes with the threshold. The main detection crosses when the largest change over
# 0 to 200 ms exceeds t times the baseline SD of the mean SDF; the t that gives a pseudo-onset rate
# of 0.01 is read off the pseudo-onset distribution of that ratio and applied at the true onset.
z_pseudo = pm.max_abs_z.fillna(-np.inf).values
t_main = stats.t.ppf(1 - stretch.P_THRESHOLD / 2, int(np.diff(stretch.BASELINE_MS)[0]) - 1)
t_cal = float(np.quantile(z_pseudo, 0.99))
print(f"t of the main detection {t_main:.2f}; t giving a pseudo-onset rate of 0.01: {t_cal:.2f}")
cal_rows = []
for (cell, d), m in mean_sdf.items():
    for shift in (0, stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS):
        q = stretch.detect(m[None, :], shift_ms=shift, tcrit=t_cal)
        cal_rows.append({"cell": cell, "direction": d, "pseudo": shift != 0, "responds": q["responds"],
                         "any_crossing_0_200": q["any_crossing_0_200"]})
cal = pd.DataFrame(cal_rows)
print(cal.groupby("pseudo")[["any_crossing_0_200", "responds"]].mean().round(4).to_string())
cal_cell = cal[~cal.pseudo].groupby("cell").responds.any()
first_overall = main.assign(early=main.first_crossing < stretch.ONSET_RANGE_MS[0])
print(f"\nDetected responses (main) with an earlier crossing at 0 to {stretch.ONSET_RANGE_MS[0] - 1} ms: "
      f"{int((first_overall.responds & first_overall.early).sum())} of {int(main.responds.sum())}")
fo_cell = first_overall.assign(r=first_overall.responds & ~first_overall.early).groupby("cell").r.any()
rows = []
for label, rel in (("main", cells.torque_related), ("calibrated threshold", cal_cell.reindex(cells.index)),
                   ("first crossing overall in 20 to 60 ms", fo_cell.reindex(cells.index))):
    for g in ("M1", "PTN", "CSN"):
        sub = cells.index if g == "M1" else cells.index[cells.ptype == g]
        for st in ("pre", "post"):
            idx = [k for k in sub if cells.state[k] == st]
            rows.append({"detection": label, "group": g, "state": st, "percent": 100 * rel[idx].mean(),
                         "expected": {('M1', 'pre'): 75, ('M1', 'post'): 68, ('PTN', 'pre'): 55, ('PTN', 'post'): 68, ('CSN', 'pre'): 45, ('CSN', 'post'): 21}[(g, st)]})

Result: blocked (methods underspecified). With the detection fixed in the claims file, a threshold crossing in the 200 ms after a pseudo onset 600 ms before the torque occurs in 0.22 of the cell-directions, against the 0.01 the paper's threshold implies; the t-test variant gives 0.46. Unperturbed trials at the usual torque time give 0.19 and 0.45, and stationary Poisson spike trains at each cell-direction's baseline rate give 0.15 and 0.49, so most of the excess comes from the detection procedure; for the main detection about a third of the observed 0.22 is not explained by the Poisson trains. The rate does not fall with baseline rate or number of trials (0.17 to 0.27 by baseline rate quartile, 0.21 to 0.24 by number of trials). A response with onset between 20 and 60 ms is found in 0.044 of the cell-directions at the pseudo onset and 0.047 on unperturbed trials, against 0.37 at the true onset, a ratio of 0.12. Fourteen cell-directions (10 of them CSNs) have no spike in the baseline and can never respond. Both rates are more than 3 times the paper's, so the procedure here differs from the paper's in a way its Methods do not settle, and the claims that rest on the selection of responses are blocked with the same reason. This analysis cannot tell whether the paper's procedure differs or its stated rate does not hold. A threshold calibrated to a pseudo-onset rate of 0.01 (t = 6.67 against 3.11) finds 30.4% and 32.7% of M1 cells torque-related, further from the paper's 75% and 68%; taking the first crossing anywhere in 0 to 200 ms as the onset removes 6 of the 202 responses. The analyses of the blocked claims are run below all the same, and their numbers are reported.

torque-related-fractions¶

In monkey V, 84 of 112 M1 neurons (75%) were torque-related before MPTP and 108 of 159 (68%) after; PTNs 27 of 49 (55%) and 37 of 54 (68%); CSNs 14 of 31 (45%) and 10 of 48 (21%).

def related_table(df, label):
    rows = []
    for (g, st), e in expected_frac.items():
        sub = df if g == "M1" else df[df.ptype == g]
        sub = sub[sub.state == st]
        k, n = int(sub.torque_related.sum()), len(sub)
        rows.append({"detection": label, "group": g, "state": st, "related": k, "n": n,
                     "percent": 100 * k / n, "expected": e, "in_tol": abs(100 * k / n - e) <= 0.1 * e})
    return rows

                          + related_table(cells.assign(torque_related=cells.torque_related_trials), "t-test variant")

prevalence-unchanged¶

MPTP did not change the fraction of torque-related neurons, in M1, in PTNs or in CSNs (chi-square, p > 0.05/3).

In [20]:
def chi2_yates(a_k, a_n, b_k, b_n):
    table = np.array([[a_k, a_n - a_k], [b_k, b_n - b_k]])
    chi2, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=True)
    return chi2, p


rows = []
for label, col in (("main", "torque_related"), ("t-test variant", "torque_related_trials")):
    for g in ("M1", "PTN", "CSN"):
        sub = cells if g == "M1" else cells[cells.ptype == g]
        a, b = sub[sub.state == "pre"][col], sub[sub.state == "post"][col]
        chi2, p = chi2_yates(a.sum(), len(a), b.sum(), len(b))
        rows.append({"detection": label, "group": g, "pre_%": 100 * a.mean(), "post_%": 100 * b.mean(),
                     "change_points": 100 * (b.mean() - a.mean()), "chi2": chi2, "p": p, "p_below_0.05/3": p < 0.05 / 3})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe paper's monkey V counts, through the same test:",

ptn-more-responsive¶

PTNs responded to torque more often than CSNs (68% against 31%, chi-square 32.3, p < 0.001).

In [21]:
for label, col in (("main", "torque_related"), ("t-test variant", "torque_related_trials")):
    p_, c_ = cells[cells.ptype == "PTN"][col], cells[cells.ptype == "CSN"][col]
    chi2, p = chi2_yates(p_.sum(), len(p_), c_.sum(), len(c_))
    print(f"{label}: PTN {int(p_.sum())}/{len(p_)} ({100 * p_.mean():.1f}%), CSN {int(c_.sum())}/{len(c_)} "
          f"({100 * c_.mean():.1f}%), chi-square {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.2e}; expected 62.1% and 30.4%")

main: PTN 71/103 (68.9%), CSN 13/79 (16.5%), chi-square 47.5, p = 5.64e-12; expected 62.1% and 30.4%
t-test variant: PTN 62/103 (60.2%), CSN 26/79 (32.9%), chi-square 12.3, p = 4.64e-04; expected 62.1% and 30.4%

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). PTNs respond more often than CSNs (68.9% against 16.5%, chi-square 47.5, p = 5.6e-12); both fractions are outside tolerance, the PTN fraction above the expected 62.1 +/- 6.2% and the CSN fraction below the expected 30.4 +/- 3.0%.

one-direction-half¶

About half of the torque-related cells (124 of 284, 44%) responded to only one direction.

excitatory-majority¶

Most torque responses were increases in firing (86% and 88% of M1 responses; 70% and 75% for PTNs), and MPTP did not change the PTN balance (chi-square 0.1, p = 0.7).

In [23]:
rows = []
for g in ("M1", "PTN", "CSN"):
    sub = resp if g == "M1" else resp[resp.ptype == g]
    for st in ("pre", "post"):
        x = sub[sub.state == st]
        rows.append({"group": g, "state": st, "increases": int((x.sign > 0).sum()), "responses": len(x),
                     "percent": 100 * (x.sign > 0).mean(),
                     "flexion": f"{int(((x.sign > 0) & (x.direction == 'flexion')).sum())}/{int((x.direction == 'flexion').sum())}",
                     "extension": f"{int(((x.sign > 0) & (x.direction == 'extension')).sum())}/{int((x.direction == 'extension').sum())}"})
inc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(inc.round(1).to_string(index=False))
for g in ("PTN", "CSN"):
    a, b = inc[(inc.group == g) & (inc.state == "pre")].iloc[0], inc[(inc.group == g) & (inc.state == "post")].iloc[0]
    chi2, p = chi2_yates(a.increases, a.responses, b.increases, b.responses)
    print(f"{g} increases pre against post: chi-square {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}")
print("All responses, both states:", f"{100 * (resp.sign > 0).mean():.1f}% increases of {len(resp)}")
chi2, p = chi2_yates(23, 24, 19, 22)

magnitude-unchanged and venus-response-magnitudes¶

The magnitude of torque responses did not differ before and after MPTP, for M1 cells or for PTNs, by any of three measures (Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Mann-Whitney, all p > 0.15).

In monkey V the mean response magnitudes were 42.4 and 37.9 spikes/s (M1 flexion), 50.9 and 42.6 (M1 extension), 33.4 and 26.1 (PTN flexion), 38.8 and 29.3 (PTN extension).

latency-shorter¶

Response latencies were shorter after MPTP for M1 cells and for PTNs, for flexion and extension (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, all p < 0.05). Monkey V means 39.2 and 34.6 ms (M1 flexion), 40.4 and 33.4 (M1 extension), 43.9 and 35.5 (PTN flexion), 44.4 and 36.7 (PTN extension).

In [26]:
expected_lat = {("M1", "flexion"): (39.2, 34.56), ("M1", "extension"): (40.4, 33.4),
                ("PTN", "flexion"): (43.9, 35.5), ("PTN", "extension"): (44.4, 36.7)}


def latency_table(rsp):
    rows = []
    for (g, d), (e_pre, e_post) in expected_lat.items():
        sub = rsp if g == "M1" else rsp[rsp.ptype == g]
        x = sub[sub.direction == d]
        a, b = x[x.state == "pre"].latency, x[x.state == "post"].latency
        rows.append({"group": g, "direction": d, "n_pre": len(a), "pre": a.mean(), "expected_pre": e_pre,
                     "in_tol_pre": abs(a.mean() - e_pre) <= 0.1 * e_pre, "n_post": len(b), "post": b.mean(),
                     "expected_post": e_post, "in_tol_post": abs(b.mean() - e_post) <= 0.1 * e_post,
                     "ks_p": stats.ks_2samp(a, b).pvalue, "mwu_p": mwu(a, b)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


lat = latency_table(resp)
print(lat.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nPooled means (paper, both monkeys: M1 41 and 35 ms, PTN 46 and 38 ms):")
for g in ("M1", "PTN"):
    sub = resp if g == "M1" else resp[resp.ptype == g]
    cs = cells[cells.torque_related] if g == "M1" else cells[cells.torque_related & (cells.ptype == g)]
    print(f"  {g}: responses {sub[sub.state == 'pre'].latency.mean():.1f} and {sub[sub.state == 'post'].latency.mean():.1f} ms; "
          f"earliest per cell {cs[cs.state == 'pre'].latency.mean():.1f} and {cs[cs.state == 'post'].latency.mean():.1f} ms "
          f"(KS p = {stats.ks_2samp(cs[cs.state == 'pre'].latency, cs[cs.state == 'post'].latency).pvalue:.4f})")
resp_t = R[(R.method == "trials") & ~R.pseudo & R.responds]

print(latency_table(resp_t)[["group", "direction", "n_pre", "pre", "n_post", "post", "ks_p"]].round(4).to_string(index=False))

latency-not-training¶

Latencies did not correlate with the days of training (monkey V Spearman |rho| = 0.02, p = 0.85).

In [27]:
tr_cells = cells[cells.torque_related].copy()
first_day = sessions[sessions.subject == "Venus"].date.min()
tr_cells["day"] = (tr_cells.date - first_day).dt.days
rho, p = stats.spearmanr(tr_cells.day, tr_cells.latency)
print(f"All torque-related cells (n = {len(tr_cells)}): Spearman rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}; days {tr_cells.day.min()} to {tr_cells.day.max()}")
for st in ("pre", "post"):
    x = tr_cells[tr_cells.state == st]
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(x.day, x.latency)
    print(f"  {st}: n = {len(x)}, rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")

All torque-related cells (n = 136): Spearman rho = -0.261, p = 0.0022; days 0 to 360
  pre: n = 61, rho = 0.105, p = 0.4195
  post: n = 75, rho = -0.145, p = 0.2147

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). Latency correlates with the day of recording over both states (rho = -0.26, p = 0.0022), as post-MPTP sessions come later; within each state it does not (p = 0.42 and 0.21).

fwhm-shorter-ptn¶

Torque-evoked increases in PTN firing were briefer after MPTP (FWHM 73 to 50 ms over both monkeys; Mann-Whitney p < 0.05 for each direction). Monkey V: 97 and 52 ms (flexion), 57 and 41 ms (extension).

dsi-reduced, venus-dsi and dsi-not-baseline¶

Directional selectivity fell after MPTP; reciprocal and unidirectional responses became less common (chi-square 22.2, p < 0.001).

In monkey V the mean DSI was 0.72 and 0.66 (M1), 0.73 and 0.75 (PTN), 0.81 and 0.83 (CSN).

Pre-torque rates did not differ between directional categories (one-way ANOVA, F = 0.77, p = 0.46).

In [29]:
cats = ["reciprocal", "unidirectional", "bidirectional", "non-directional"]
tr_cells = cells[cells.torque_related]
tab = pd.crosstab(tr_cells.category, tr_cells.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
print(tab.to_string())
chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab.values)
high = tr_cells.category.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"])
fr = high.groupby(tr_cells.state).mean()
print(f"\nReciprocal or unidirectional: pre {100 * fr['pre']:.1f}%, post {100 * fr['post']:.1f}% "
      f"(change {100 * (fr['post'] - fr['pre']):.1f} points); chi-square (2 x 4) {chi2:.2f}, dof {dof}, p = {p:.4f}")
for g in ("PTN", "CSN"):
    x = tr_cells[tr_cells.ptype == g]
    t = pd.crosstab(x.category, x.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
    t = t[t.sum(axis=1) > 0]
    c2, pp, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(t.values)
    h = x.category.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"]).groupby(x.state).mean()
    print(f"  {g}: reciprocal or unidirectional pre {100 * h.get('pre', np.nan):.1f}%, post {100 * h.get('post', np.nan):.1f}%; chi-square p = {pp:.3f}")

# Variant: categories from the DSI value as the paper words them: reciprocal DSI > 1, unidirectional
# a response in one direction only (DSI <= 1), bidirectional 0.5 < DSI <= 1, non-directional DSI <= 0.5.
def by_value(r):
    if r.dsi > 1:
        return "reciprocal"
    if r.n_directions == 1:
        return "unidirectional"
    return "bidirectional" if r.dsi > 0.5 else "non-directional"


tr_v = tr_cells.assign(category_value=[by_value(r) for r in tr_cells.itertuples()])
tab_v = pd.crosstab(tr_v.category_value, tr_v.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
chi2_v, p_v, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab_v.values)
fr_v = tr_v.category_value.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"]).groupby(tr_v.state).mean()
print("\nVariant, categories by DSI value:")
print(tab_v.to_string())
print(f"Reciprocal or unidirectional: pre {100 * fr_v['pre']:.1f}%, post {100 * fr_v['post']:.1f}%; chi-square {chi2_v:.2f}, p = {p_v:.4f}")
print("Smallest expected count in the main 2 x 4 table:", round(stats.chi2_contingency(tab.values)[3].min(), 1))

Kinematics and EMG¶

Session measures use monkey V files with analog data, leaving out the four files that repeat another file's recording. Kinematics are measured on every perturbation; a trial whose joint was already moving faster than 5 deg/s in the 50 ms before onset is counted and kept.

In [32]:
kin_rows = []
for s in venus:
    if s["session_id"].split("++")[1] in set(repeats.repeated_in):
        continue
    for k, d in enumerate(s["pert_direction"]):
        r = stretch.kinematics(s["windows"]["angle"][k], d, s["analog_step_ms"])
        if r["valid"]:
            kin_rows.append({"session": s["session_id"], "post": s["post"], "direction": d, **r})
kin = pd.DataFrame(kin_rows)
kin["state"] = np.where(kin.post, "post", "pre")
print(f"{len(kin)} perturbations in {kin.session.nunique()} sessions; moving before onset: {int(kin.moving_before.sum())}; "
      f"no velocity crossing within 150 ms: {int(kin.latency_ms.isna().sum())}")
print("Ranges: latency", kin.latency_ms.min(), "to", kin.latency_ms.max(), "ms; peak velocity",
      round(kin.peak_velocity.min(), 1), "to", round(kin.peak_velocity.max(), 1), "deg/s; amplitude",
      round(kin.amplitude.min(), 2), "to", round(kin.amplitude.max(), 2), "deg")
sess_kin = kin.groupby(["session", "state", "direction"])[["latency_ms", "peak_velocity", "amplitude"]].mean().reset_index()
sess_kin["level"] = sess_kin.session.map(command.set_index("session").level)
print("\nSession means, mean over sessions:")
print(sess_kin.groupby(["direction", "state"])[["latency_ms", "peak_velocity", "amplitude"]].agg(["mean", "count"]).round(2).to_string())

kinematics-slower¶

After MPTP, torque-induced displacements were slower and smaller; mean peak velocity fell by 16.2% and amplitude by 6.6% (ANOVA, F > 515 and F > 49).

In [33]:
def anova(df, measure):
    model = ols(f"{measure} ~ C(state) * C(direction)", data=df).fit()
    return sm.stats.anova_lm(model, typ=2)


for m in ("peak_velocity", "amplitude"):
    print(f"{m}:")
    print(anova(sess_kin, m).round(4).to_string())
    print()

                   ("extension, for reference", sess_kin[sess_kin.direction == "extension"])):
    g = x.groupby("state")[["peak_velocity", "amplitude"]].mean()
    rows.append({"reading": reading, "velocity_change_%": 100 * (g.loc["post", "peak_velocity"] / g.loc["pre", "peak_velocity"] - 1),
                 "amplitude_change_%": 100 * (g.loc["post", "amplitude"] / g.loc["pre", "amplitude"] - 1)})

Absolute scale: torque-induced amplitude, mean of session means 3.09 deg (paper: about 10 deg); peak velocity 58.7 deg/s, highest session mean 145.3 (paper's matched sessions 130 to 200 deg/s). Active movements in the same files, same filter: median peak velocity 99.3 deg/s and amplitude 20.4 deg.

Result: not reproduced. In monkey V, torque-induced movements are faster and larger after MPTP: session-mean peak velocity rises by 28.8% and amplitude by 15.2% over both directions (30.3% and 12.0% for flexion), with MPTP effects F = 103 and 26 (p < 0.0001). Restricted to the sessions with the same torque command size (variant), the increase is larger (101.9% and 113.4%). The mean of the session-mean peak velocities is 58.7 deg/s, and only one response comes from a session in the paper's 130 to 200 deg/s window of matched sessions. The angle's scale matches the files' own kinematic columns (data check), so the small torque-induced movements (mean amplitude 3.09 deg, where the paper gives a mean of 10 deg) are in the data and do not come from the measure here.

Result: not reproduced. The movement onset latency is shorter after MPTP (session means 9.8 and 3.2 ms for flexion, 11.0 and 6.0 ms for extension; MPTP F = 1032, p < 0.0001), with an MPTP by direction interaction (F = 19.1). In the sessions with the same command size (variant) it does not differ (7.81 and 7.73 ms, p = 0.79). The zero-phase filter can move an onset earlier, and 219 of 5413 perturbations have a latency of 0 ms. With a causal 10 ms average of the unfiltered velocity, which cannot move it earlier, the session means are 12.6 to 18.6 ms and still shorter after MPTP (F = 781); leaving out the trials already moving before onset gives F = 1037 (filtered) and 743 (causal). At the middle command size the causal variant gives p = 0.25, and p = 0.026 without the trials moving before onset. The latency difference goes with the torque command, so it cannot be attributed to MPTP; the outcome is the criterion's comparison.

EMG¶

Session-average responses of the three triceps channels to flexion torques, which stretch the triceps, with the extension torques shown for the contrast.

In [35]:
emg_rows, traces = [], {}
for s in venus:
    code_ = s["session_id"].split("++")[1]
    if code_ in set(repeats.repeated_in):
        continue
    for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3]:
        if ch not in s["windows"]:
            continue
        w = s["windows"][ch]
        if np.isnan(w).any() or np.nanstd(w[:, AX < 0]) < 1:
            continue
        for d in ("flexion", "extension"):
            r = stretch.emg_response(w[s["pert_direction"] == d], s["analog_step_ms"])
            emg_rows.append({"session": code_, "post": s["post"], "channel": ch, "direction": d,
                             **{k: r[k] for k in ("m1", "m2", "onset_ms", "duration_ms")}})
            traces[(code_, ch, d)] = r["trace"]
emg = pd.DataFrame(emg_rows)
emg["state"] = np.where(emg.post, "post", "pre")
emg["level"] = emg.session.map(command.set_index("code").level)

  EMGTricepsLateralis: n 16 and 1, median m2 19.66 and 0.52, KS p = 0.1176

Result: reproduced. For flexion torques, the m2 response is larger after MPTP in all three triceps channels (medians 3.0 against 164.2, 3.1 against 297.5 and 5.2 against 76.2 A/D units; Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 1e-10 for each). The increase follows the torque command: in sessions of the middle command size (variant), m2 is not larger after MPTP (triceps longus 1 median 46.7 against 1.3, p = 0.013, in the opposite direction). By command size and state the median m2 is 0.61 at the smallest size (pre only), 40.8 (pre) and 1.81 (post) at the middle, and 17.09 (pre, n = 5) and 194.6 (post) at the largest, so it does not rise simply with command size within a state. As the torque command is about four times larger in most post-MPTP sessions, the increase cannot be attributed to MPTP; the outcome is the criterion's comparison.

emg-duration-longer and emg-onset-unchanged¶

The total duration of EMG responses to torque increased after MPTP, from 57 +/- 6 to 79 +/- 3 ms (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.001). The latency of the earliest EMG responses did not change.

Result: partially reproduced. EMG responses last longer after MPTP (24.5 against 50.4 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 1.8e-39), but both means are outside tolerance (expected 57 and 79 ms); thresholds of 1.5 and 3 SD give the same direction (16.4 against 48.5 and 17.3 against 49.5 ms). At the middle command size (variant) the durations do not differ (28.4 and 27.9 ms, p = 0.96). Before MPTP 63.6% of the durations are 10 ms or less (median 9 ms, against 59 ms after), so many pre-MPTP responses are brief crossings of a small signal.

Result: not reproduced. The onset of the EMG response is earlier after MPTP (40.8 against 24.0 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 5.5e-21), with the same direction at thresholds of 1.5 and 3 SD. At the middle command size (variant) the onsets do not differ (28.8 and 45.6 ms, p = 0.18), the post-MPTP onset being the later one there.

emg-m1-weak¶

The short-latency m1 component (15 to 40 ms) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than m2.

pre: m2 > m1 in 73.5% of 310 channel-sessions; median m1 0.38, median m2 3.18, median m1/m2 0.10 (over channel-sessions with m2 > 0: 0.09)
post: m2 > m1 in 96.5% of 282 channel-sessions; median m1 40.65, median m2 191.67, median m1/m2 0.22 (over channel-sessions with m2 > 0: 0.23)

Result: partially reproduced. After MPTP m2 exceeds m1 in 96.5% of channel-sessions with a median m1 / m2 of 0.22 (0.23 over channel-sessions with m2 > 0). Before MPTP the median ratio is 0.10 (0.09 with m2 > 0), but m2 exceeds m1 in 73.5%, just below the 75% of the criterion.

velocity-matched-magnitude¶

In sessions with equivalent torque-induced velocities (130 to 200 deg/s), MPTP did not change the magnitude of responses (Mann-Whitney, p = 0.19 and 0.46; 24 and 33 flexion, 22 and 31 extension responses).

session-correlations¶

Across sessions, the mean PTN latency did not correlate with peak velocity (|rho| < 0.18) or with the m2 EMG response (|rho| < 0.26; Spearman, threshold 0.05/4).

In [40]:

ptn_cells["session"] = [S[si]["session_id"] for si in ptn_cells.si]

per_session["m2"] = per_session.code.map(m2)

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). Over sessions, mean PTN latency does not reach the paper's threshold with velocity (rho = -0.22, p = 0.080) and does with the triceps longus 1 m2 (rho = -0.32, p = 0.011, below 0.0125); within each state neither correlates (p 0.36 to 0.997).

trial-correlations¶

Trial by trial, PTN response latencies did not correlate with the peak velocity or the m2 EMG response (Spearman |rho| < 0.34, p > 0.05).

Blocked: the Methods define response onset on the trial-averaged SDF and give no way of measuring a latency on a single trial, which this test needs.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Only monkey V is analysed, as the monkey L files mark no torque perturbation; the paper pools both monkeys except in its supplementary table. The response detection is one reading of the Methods (a threshold on the trial-averaged SDF set from the baseline's SD), with a t-test across trials as a variant. Its false-positive rate over the 200 ms epoch is about 0.2, not the 0.01 the paper's threshold implies, and Poisson spike trains give 0.15, most of it, so the claims that rest on the selection of responses are blocked, though their analyses ran. A threshold calibrated to a false-positive rate of 0.01 finds fewer torque-related cells, further from the paper's. With this detection the latency shortening after MPTP appears with the paper's monkey V means, but the response magnitudes fall after MPTP, which the paper did not find. The kinematic and EMG measures follow the Methods where they are given; the response windows, the EMG threshold and the peak velocity window are choices made here. The analog streams are realigned to the trials table. The torque command differs in size between the states, so the kinematic and EMG differences found here cannot be attributed to MPTP, whatever their outcome on the criteria.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • The monkey L files mark no torque perturbation, so the monkey L half of the paper (115 and 73 cells) cannot be tested; the Leu torque command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file, 15 post-MPTP Leu files have no analog data, and in the other post-MPTP files the command moves during the active movements, with one excursion in a hold window in 2048 trials.
  • The analog streams (angle, torque command, EMG) are stored on a clock that falls about 5 ms per trial behind the trials table and the spikes, reaching hundreds of ms; realigned per trial, the torque command steps 4 to 7 ms after every labelled onset.
  • The torque command's pulse is about four times larger in most post-MPTP sessions than in most pre-MPTP sessions (183 against 46 units, with 91 in some sessions of both), and post-MPTP pulses are followed by an opposite swing; the paper describes one 0.1 Nm, 50 ms impulse. The command's scale is not given, so this may be a change of torque or of the command's recording; the kinematic and EMG results differ between the sessions of different command sizes.
  • The angle's reference frame says positive is extension; the data show positive is flexion. The series are named "Elbow" also for monkey L, whose task used the wrist.
  • Four files repeat a block of another file's recording; in two of them the same unit, with identical spikes, is stored twice with different projection types.
  • unit_also_in_session_id uses prefixes ("V", "L") that differ from the session ids, mostly names files that are not in the dandiset, and where the file is present it points to a different unit.
  • The monkey L analog streams are at 100 Hz (the paper says 200 Hz). The dandiset description says MPTP was systemic (the files and the paper say intracarotid), that the task used the elbow in both monkeys, and that Leu was recorded in 1993 (some files are from 1992).
  • The torque onset comes 1.70 to 1.73 s after the center target appears in 90% of perturbations, where the Methods describe an onset 1 to 2 s after center capture, at random.
  • The angle's scale agrees with the files' own movement amplitudes and peak velocities; the torque-induced movements (about 3 deg) are smaller than the paper's mean of 10 deg.
  • The monkey V cells with at least 5 perturbations per direction match the paper's monkey V counts of cells, PTNs and CSNs exactly, so the selection of cells can be recovered.
